files.lesson.md: --- order: 18 unit: samples node: AC9M8ST02 n2 uses: [AC9M8ST02 n1, AC9M7ST02 n2] title: Describing a sample summary: "Display a sample's data, then report its shape, centre and spread, and what it suggests about the population: an estimate, with the sampling method and size stated." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A news story says 'Teens sleep 8 hours a night.' Is that every teen, most teens, or a sample's average? A good report says which, and how the sample was chosen." connection: canteen-sample # data/connections/maths.yml (documentation only) app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8336 url: http://127.0.0.1:8336/index.html readySelector: "#gsum" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: board.yml#explain-pic, caption: "A random sample of 40 students' sleep: most between 8 and 10 hours, a few lower. The dashed line is the whole school's mean." } explainClip: query: { code: "@board.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Reporting on a sample" say: "Shape, centre and spread, then what it suggests." clip: - caption: { text: "Take a random sample of 40 and plot their sleep.", say: "Take a random sample of forty and plot their sleep." } - click: Take a sample - expect: { selector: "#gnote", contains: "median" } - caption: { text: "Report the shape, the centre (mean, median) and the spread (range).", say: "Report its shape, its centre and its spread." } - wait: 1800 - caption: { text: "Then: about this much for the school, from a random sample of 40.", say: "Then say what it suggests for the whole school." } - wait: 1400 --- A **report** on a sample describes its **distribution**, then says what it suggests about the population: - **shape**: symmetric (balanced about the middle), skewed (a long tail to one side), any clusters, gaps or outliers - **centre**: the mean and median - **spread**: the range (highest − lowest) - **what it suggests**: an estimate for the population, with how the sample was chosen and its size Data you collect yourself is **primary** data; data someone else collected (the ABS, a website, a study) is **secondary** data. ## Predict: the shape ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to the shape of 40 students' sleep shows whether they expect real data to cluster." check: type: predict q: "You plot the hours of sleep of 40 students chosen at random. What will the dot plot look like?" options: ["Most dots in the middle, fewer towards the ends", "Dots spread evenly from lowest to highest", "Every dot at the same value"] actual: "Most in the middle, fewer at the ends: most students sleep a similar amount, and a few sleep much more or less." ``` ## Run: a sample of 40 ```step stage: run insight: "Taking a random sample and reading its dot plot and statistics gives the raw material for a report." try: { playground: board, starter: "board.yml#run", height: 720 } check: { type: board, text: "Take a random sample of 40. Describe its shape, and read its mean, median and range. Was its shape what you predicted?", when: "k = 1 and s >= 1", explain: "Most values sit between about 8 and 10 hours. The mean and median are close, so the shape is roughly symmetric." } ``` ## Investigate: from data to report ```step stage: investigate insight: "Find the centre and spread of a sample; a sample's mean is an estimate, not the population's exact value (Leo); primary and secondary data both need their source." tasks: - check: type: number q: "A sample of 7 students' sleep: 8.0, 9.5, 10.0, 7.5, 9.0, 8.5, 9.0 hours. What is the median, in hours?" answer: 9 tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["7.5", "That is the middle of the list as written. Put them in order first: 7.5, 8.0, 8.5, 9.0, 9.0, 9.5, 10.0."] explain: "In order, the 4th of 7 is 9.0 hours." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#leo" text: "Leo reports on his sample. Click the line where his report goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: sample-is-population explain: "Line 2: a sample's mean estimates the population's; it isn't exactly the same. He should write 'about 8.9 hours, from a random sample of 30'." - check: type: question q: "A student uses ABS figures on screen time from a national survey. What kind of data is this?" options: ["Secondary data: someone else collected it", "Primary data: she is using it", "A census", "An experiment"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Primary data is collected by you.", "A survey of some people is a sample.", "Nothing was changed on purpose."] explain: "Secondary data is collected by others. Say where it came from and how it was collected." ``` ### Median Here is the routine for a report. ```worked \text{Random sample of } 20 \text{ Year 8s: minutes reading per day} :: Say the sample: method and size. \text{Shape: most } 10 \text{ to } 30,\ \text{one outlier at } 120 :: Describe the shape. \text{Median } 20,\ \text{mean } 25,\ \text{range } 120 - 5 = 115 :: Centre and spread (the outlier pulls the mean up). \text{Year 8s read about } 20 \text{ minutes a day} :: An estimate for the population, with its limits. ``` ### Find the mistake Read Leo's report. Did he measure all 200 students? ### Primary or secondary ## Modify: compare and report ```step stage: modify insight: "A stratified sample's plot, and two samples side by side, show how to compare centres and spreads in a report." try: { playground: board, starter: "board.yml#two", height: 720 } tasks: - starter: "board.yml#strat" check: { type: board, text: "Take a stratified sample of 40 (10 from each year). Describe its shape. Is its mean close to the school's mean?", when: "k = 3 and s >= 1", explain: "A stratified sample has each year's fair share, so its centre is usually close to the school's." } - starter: "board.yml#two" check: type: question q: "The plot shows a sample of 15 Year 7s (top) and 15 Year 10s (bottom). Which is true?" options: ["Year 7s sleep more: their median is about 1 hour higher", "Year 10s sleep more", "They sleep the same", "You can't compare samples"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Look at where the middle of each plot sits.", "The middles are about an hour apart.", "Comparing centres and spreads is how samples are compared."] explain: "Year 7's median is 9.0 hours and Year 10's is 8.0 hours." - starter: "board.yml#two" check: type: number q: "What is the range of the Year 10 sample, in hours?" answer: 3 tolerance: 0 explain: "Highest 9.5, lowest 6.5: 9.5 − 6.5 = 3 hours." - check: type: question q: "Which sentence is the best report for the Year 10 sample?" options: ["In a random sample of 15 Year 10s, the median sleep was 8 hours (range 3 hours), so Year 10s at this school sleep about 8 hours", "All Year 10s sleep 8 hours", "Year 10s sleep badly", "The data shows 15 numbers"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Not all: the values vary, and it is a sample.", "That is an opinion, not a summary.", "That describes nothing about the data."] explain: "A report gives the sample, the centre and spread, and an estimate for the population." ``` ### Stratified sample ### Compare two samples ### Spread ### The best report ## Practise: describing samples ```step stage: practise insight: "Centre, spread, shape and claims about the population, mixed; treating a sample's mean as exact is the planted slip; sampling methods are the review." tasks: - check: type: number q: "A sample's values are 4, 6, 6, 7, 9, 10, 14. What is the mean?" answer: 8 tolerance: 0 explain: "Total 56 ÷ 7 = 8." - check: type: question q: "A sample's dot plot has most values between 2 and 5, and a long tail of a few values up to 15. How would you describe its shape?" options: ["Skewed: a long tail to the high side", "Symmetric", "Evenly spread", "Two clusters"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "One side has a long tail, so it isn't balanced.", "Most values are bunched together.", "There is one main group."] explain: "A tail stretching to the high values is skewed to the right (positively skewed); the mean is pulled above the median." - check: type: question q: "From a random sample of 50 students, 30 walk to school. What is the best claim about the school?" options: ["About 60% of the school's students walk to school", "Exactly 60% walk", "30 students walk", "Nobody can say anything"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "A sample gives an estimate.", "That is only the sample.", "A random sample gives a reasonable estimate."] explain: "30/50 = 60% is an estimate for the school: 'about 60%'." - check: type: question q: "Review: a club has 60 members listed alphabetically. Which gives a systematic sample of 10?" options: ["Every 6th member from a random start", "The first 10 on the list", "10 chosen from a hat", "10 from each age group"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That is convenience, and names near A may differ.", "That is simple random.", "That is stratified (or quota)."] explain: "60 ÷ 10 = 6: every 6th from a random start." ``` ### Mean ### Shape ### A claim about the school ### Review: systematic ## Make: your report ```step stage: make insight: "Taking a fair sample and writing a full report shows they can analyse and report on a sample distribution." try: { playground: board, starter: "board.yml#make", height: 720 } hint: ["Choose a fair method and a size, then take one sample.", "Report: the sample, the shape, the centre, the spread, and an estimate for the school."] check: { type: board, text: "Choose a fair method and a sample size, and take a sample. Then write your report.", when: "k < 4 and s >= 1", explain: "A fair method gives a sample you can report on. Check your estimate against the dashed line." } ``` Write a short report: the method and size, the shape, the mean, median and range, and what it suggests about how much the school's students sleep. Then compare your estimate with the dashed line. ## Make: on paper ```step stage: make insight: "Reporting a made-up canteen sample's mean as an estimate for the school, with the reason picked at the key step." check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "The canteen asks a random sample of 8 students how many lunches they bought there last week (made up): 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6. Find the mean, then say what it tells the canteen about all 900 students. Work it out on paper." steps: - ["$2 + 3 + 3 + 4 + 4 + 5 + 5 + 6 = 32$", "add all 8 values"] - ["$32 \\div 8 = 4$", "divide by how many values: the sample's mean"] - ["The school's mean is about 4 lunches a week, from a random sample of 8", "a sample gives an estimate, and the report says how the sample was chosen"] picks: - step: 3 q: "Why say 'about 4' and name the sample?" options: ["A random sample estimates the school's mean, but another sample would give a slightly different value", "Every student buys exactly 4 lunches", "The sample's mean is the school's mean, because the sample is part of the school"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The values run from 2 to 6: the mean is the centre, not every student.", "A sample is only part of the school, so its mean is an estimate."] answer: "4" answerLabel: "Mean (lunches a week)" tolerance: 0.01 feedback: - ["32", "That is the total. Divide by the 8 students."] - ["4.5", "That is the middle of 3 and 6, not the mean of all 8 values."] criteria: - "I added all 8 values before dividing." - "I divided by 8, the number of students in the sample." - "My sentence says 'about' and says how the sample was chosen." explain: "32 ÷ 8 = 4. A random sample of 8 suggests the school's mean is about 4 lunches a week, give or take." ``` Do this one in your book or on paper, one step per line, before you type the number. **Also used in** - **The canteen.** A canteen asks a sample of students, then reports the typical answer and the spread for the whole school. - **News stories.** 'Teens sleep 8 hours' is a sample's centre. A good report says how the sample was chosen. - **Class work.** Take your own sample and write the report. ```teacher summary: Students take samples of a simulated school, describe each sample's shape, centre and spread, compare two samples, and report an estimate with its method and size (AC9M8ST02, node 2). time: 40 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 10 min · Modify 12 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can describe a sample's shape, centre and spread. - I can compare two samples by their centres and spreads. - I can write a report that gives an estimate for the population and says how the sample was chosen. struggle: "Writing 'about' and saying how the sample was chosen. Ask: is this every student, or a sample? How was it picked?" before: > Do the Run board yourself first. Students need mean, median, range and dot plots (Year 7) and sampling methods (last lesson). The one idea: a report describes the sample (shape, centre, spread) and then estimates the population, naming the method and size. The common mistake is reporting a sample's mean as the population's exact value (Leo's mistake). The board plots the sample's values (rounded to 0.2 h) and gives the mean, median and range; the dashed line is the school's mean, for checking afterwards. Primary data: collected by the student; secondary: by others (ABS, studies). Wider: find a secondary source (ABS or a health survey) on teenagers' sleep and compare it with the school sample. running: - "Predict: ask why the values might bunch up." - "Run: ask what the median tells you that the range doesn't." - "Investigate: ask Leo how many students he measured." - "Modify: ask how far apart the two medians are." - "Make: ask what word your estimate needs ('about')." - "Paper: the canteen mean is worked on paper; the page marks the mean and the reason for 'about', then shows a model. Books out, and look at the pages." stuck: - see: A student reports only the mean. ask: How spread out are the values? What shape? fix: Shape, centre and spread, every time. - see: A student writes the sample's mean as exact for the school. ask: Did you measure every student? fix: Write 'about', and give the method and size. - see: A student can't describe the shape. ask: Where do most dots sit? Is one side longer? fix: Symmetric, or skewed towards the long tail; mention clusters, gaps and outliers. stretch: Take five samples of 40 and write each mean. How much do they vary? (Next lesson investigates this.) support: "A report frame: 'In a [method] sample of [n], the values were mostly [..]. The median was [..] and the range [..]. So the school's students probably [..].'" leads: | This completes AC9M8ST02. Where it leads: how samples vary (next), and full investigations with samples. exit: q: A random sample of 25 students spends a median of 40 minutes on homework a night (range 0 to 120). Write one sentence about the school. a: Students at the school probably spend about 40 minutes on homework a night, though some spend much more, based on a random sample of 25. explain: > To **report** on a sample: describe its **shape** (symmetric or skewed, clusters, outliers), **centre** (mean, median) and **spread** (range). Then give an **estimate** for the population, with the sampling method and size, using words like "about". **Primary** data you collect yourself; **secondary** data someone else collected. Either way, say where it came from. ```

files.working.txt:
# Leo's report for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: leo
Leo takes a random sample of 30 students and finds their mean sleep is 8.9 hours.
He reports: "The mean sleep of all 200 students is exactly 8.9 hours."
He adds that the sample was chosen at random from the school roll.
# endregion
